## Local community: the guardians of the Charca

Saturday morning begins with a group of volunteers putting up signs along the main path. They wear reflective vests, work gloves, and that familiarity with the terrain that can only be acquired after hundreds of hours walking among reeds and tamarisks. They are members of the Association of Friends of the Charca de Suárez, an organization founded in 1998 that today has more than two hundred members and serves as the living memory of this wetland.

The association was born when the Charca did not appear on tourist maps or in the budget priorities of any administration. A group of local residents, naturalists, and teachers began meeting to document the biological richness of a space that many considered a simple damp wasteland. Those early field outings, with notebooks and bird guides, laid the foundations of a citizens' movement that would eventually demonstrate its capacity for influence.

The most decisive moment came in 2005, when the construction of a golf course on the wetland's land was proposed. The association launched a mobilization campaign that included petition drives, public appearances, and intense outreach work in local and regional media. The neighborhood pressure, articulated with ecological arguments and rigorous data on the species present, managed to halt the project and placed the Charca at the center of the debate on urban development on the Granada coast.

Since then, the relationship with the Motril City Council has evolved toward stable collaboration. Volunteers participate in organizing open house days, design guided routes for schoolchildren and families, and maintain a constant presence in environmental awareness campaigns. Their knowledge of the terrain is especially valuable for detecting changes in water levels, the appearance of invasive species, or any alteration that a casual observer would overlook.

Citizen surveillance constitutes one of the least visible but most constant functions of the association. Members walk the perimeter of the wetland in informal shifts, report incidents to municipal technicians, and act as eyes and ears for a space that does not always have sufficient staff for its daily custody. This silent work has made it possible to document occasional discharges, detect the presence of visitors who strayed from authorized paths, and alert about prolonged drought episodes affecting the shallowest lagoons.

The motto the association has made its own, "The Charca belongs to everyone," summarizes a philosophy that goes beyond mere advocacy. The organization's members insist that the wetland does not belong to any administration or interest group, but constitutes a collective heritage that must be passed on in good condition to future generations. This idea of shared ownership explains the emotional involvement of the volunteers, many of whom have watched their children grow up participating in the environmental education activities organized on the premises.

Outreach work also extends to the digital sphere, where the association maintains active social media profiles and a periodic newsletter with information on sightings, activities, and news about the management of the space. Photographs of migratory birds, maps of recommended routes, and notices about temporary closures of observation points circulate quickly among a community of followers that transcends the local area. Ornithologists from other provinces regularly consult these channels before planning their visits.

The relationship with educational centers in Motril and the Costa Tropical region constitutes another pillar of the association's activity. Volunteers accompany school groups on routes adapted to each age, explaining in simple terms the water cycles, the function of reed beds as bird refuges, and the importance of not feeding wildlife. Many children in the area have had their first contact with a purple swamphen or a kingfisher through a member of the Charca.

Generational renewal is a concern the association addresses with realism. In recent years, the board of directors has promoted the incorporation of younger profiles, with special attention to biology, environmental science, and tourism students who see the Charca as a natural laboratory to complete their training. The scientific bird-ringing sessions, organized in collaboration with specialists, have proven to be an effective tool for attracting new volunteers interested in field ornithology.

Collaboration with the City Council is formalized through agreements that define the areas of joint action. The association contributes volunteering and specialized knowledge, while the municipality provides infrastructure, materials, and coordination with the wetland's technical staff. This co-management model, while not perfect, has made it possible to multiply public-use activities without the local administration having to bear the cost of organization and outreach alone.

The most veteran members recall with pride the transformations of the space: the recovery of lagoons that were on the verge of silting up, the installation of accessible observation points, the consolidation of a breeding colony of purple herons that today constitutes one of the most important on the Andalusian coast. Each improvement is perceived as a collective achievement, as confirmation that the 2005 citizens' mobilization was not an isolated episode but the beginning of a lasting commitment.

The association maintains a vigilant attitude toward the new challenges on the horizon. Urban development pressure on the surroundings, water scarcity during drought periods, and the arrival of invasive exotic species are matters the volunteers follow closely and bring to the attention of the competent administrations when they consider it necessary. Their role as a critical counterweight has not disappeared, although it is now exercised from a position of greater institutional dialogue.

The work of the guardians of the Charca is clearly perceived in everyday details: a newly placed sign indicating the presence of Kentish plover nests, a railing repaired after a storm, a group of schoolchildren learning to distinguish the song of the Cetti's warbler. These are small gestures that, added together, build a culture of respect toward a space that was on the verge of disappearing under concrete and that today is consolidated as a benchmark of biodiversity on the Granada coast.
